## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Stopping Times and Online Algorithms
  Official title       Stopping times and online algorithms
  Instructors          V. PERCHET (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 24 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Theory
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com course description is written in English)
  Assessment           Written exam (master-mva.com) · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” · weights not displayed
  Prerequisites        “There are no real prerequisites, the course is more or less self-contained” (master-mva.com)
  Note on sources      master-mva.com lists the course in semester 2; the Université Paris-Saclay table places it in semester 1
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or economics who is at ease with probability and linear programming, and who wants to learn how to decide *when* to act while the data arrive one at a time.

**Empirical first**: interview 100 candidates in a uniformly random order and hire on the spot or never. Rejecting the first 37 and then taking the first candidate better than all of them hires the very best one 37.1 % of the time, and 37.0 % of 100,000 simulated orders agree. On a ski trip of unknown length, renting until the rent paid reaches the price of the skis and then buying never costs more than twice the hindsight optimum. This course explains both numbers, and many more of the same kind.

The course studies algorithms that discover the data one item after the other and must commit at once, with decisions that weigh on the future: a budget spent, a vertex matched, a server moved. Their quality is measured against an offline optimum that knows everything in advance. The three families of problems are stopping problems (secretaries, prophets, Pandora's boxes), online matching and allocation, and metrical task systems such as paging and the k-server problem. The tools are linear programming duality, stochastic approximation and reductions to trees.

It sits at the junction of probability, theoretical computer science and economics. It shares bandits and regret with [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) and dynamic programming with [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html). LP duality and mirror descent come from [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), and the transport problem from [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Define an online problem, its offline optimum and the competitive ratio of a deterministic or randomized algorithm, and tell it apart from the regret of online learning.
-   Prove upper bounds by potential functions and by weak LP duality, and lower bounds with adversarial inputs and Yao's principle.
-   Solve finite-horizon optimal stopping problems by backward induction, and the secretary problem in its classical, LP and odds forms.
-   State and prove the prophet inequality with the factor 1/2, its i.i.d. version with 1 − 1/e, and an online contention resolution scheme.
-   Derive Weitzman's index policy for Pandora's box, and turn stopping rules into posted-price mechanisms for online auctions.
-   Analyse greedy and RANKING for online bipartite matching, and the AdWords algorithm, with a randomized or deterministic primal–dual argument.
-   Learn dual prices online by stochastic approximation to allocate budgets under stochastic arrivals.
-   Analyse LRU, FIFO and marking for paging, define metrical task systems and compute work functions.
-   Prove the k lower bound for k-server and the k-competitiveness of Double Coverage on the line, and use tree embeddings to reduce a metric problem to trees.
-   Describe convex body chasing and online metric matching, and read current research papers on online decision making.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com sets the objective of understanding and mastering how to take sequential decisions that may have a strong impact on the future, typically the depletion of a budget, at the junction of mathematics, theoretical computer science and economics. The goal is to construct and analyse algorithms that discover, then treat, data one after the other rather than as a whole batch.

The quality of a sequence of decisions is compared with the optimal decisions that know everything in advance. The description announces three typical cases (prophet inequalities, online matching, metrical task systems), the main techniques (linear optimisation, stochastic approximation, tree reductions), as many open questions as possible, and a disclaimer separating online algorithms from online learning. ### Course outline

-   **Review: maxima, conditioning, linear programming and matchings** — the expectation of a maximum, independence of the future, weak duality, maximal matchings and metrics.
-   **Online algorithms and competitive analysis** — the online model, the competitive ratio, ski rental, Yao's principle, and why this is not online learning.
-   **Stopping times and the secretary problem** — filtrations, backward induction, the 1/e law, its LP and the odds theorem.
-   **Prophet inequalities** — the factor 1/2 and its proof, i.i.d. values and 1 − 1/e, random order, the ex-ante LP and contention resolution.
-   **Pandora's box, posted prices and online auctions** — Weitzman's index, its short proof, and stopping rules turned into prices.
-   **Online bipartite matching** — greedy, RANKING and its randomized primal–dual proof, and the matching upper bound.
-   **Budgets** — b-matching, AdWords, online resource allocation with learned dual prices, and matching with delays.
-   **Paging, caching and metrical task systems** — Belady, LRU, marking, and the general model with work functions.
-   **The k-server problem and tree reductions** — the k lower bound, Double Coverage, the work function algorithm, HST embeddings.
-   **Convex body chasing and online transportation** — chasing in high dimension, and online metric matching.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — the open constants, learning-augmented algorithms and the bridges with online learning (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1: the inequality on the expectation of a maximum and weak duality are used in almost every proof.
-   Keep the three questions of the course in mind for every problem: what the offline optimum is, which algorithm is proposed, and which input makes every algorithm fail.
-   Redo each central proof on paper after the session (Theorems 2.2, 3.2, 4.2, 5.3, 6.3, 7.2, 8.2 and 8.3); the written exam is likely to ask for one of them.
-   Run the Python block of each chapter and change one parameter: the size of the input, the order of arrivals, the threshold.
-   The environment is NumPy and SciPy, whose `linprog` (HiGHS solver) computes the offline LP optima; nothing else is needed.
-   Do the ★ exercises the week of the session and the ★★ proofs before the exam; the ★★★ exercises and ch. 10 point to research questions.

## 0. Review: maxima, conditioning, linear programming and matchings {#ch0}

Every proof of the course compares an online algorithm with an omniscient optimum. This chapter gathers the M1-level tools of those comparisons: the expectation of a maximum, the independence of the future, weak LP duality, matchings and metrics.

### 0.1 Expectations of maxima

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Positive part and tail formula]{.tag} For a real number $a$, write $a^+ = \max(a, 0)$. For a non-negative random variable $X$ and a level $T$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}(X > t)\, dt, \qquad \mathbb{E}[(X - T)^+] = \int_T^\infty \mathbb{P}(X > t)\, dt .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — A bound on the expected maximum]{.tag} For any random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$ (independent or not) and any level $T$,

::: key
[Key inequality — the maximum is at most a threshold plus the excesses]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{i} X_i\Big] \;\leq\; T + \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\big[(X_i - T)^+\big].
$$
:::

::: proof
Pointwise, $\max_i X_i \leq T + \max_i (X_i - T)^+$, and a maximum of non-negative numbers is at most their sum. Take expectations. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.3 — Maxima of uniform and exponential samples]{.tag} For $n$ independent uniform variables on $[0, 1]$, the maximum has distribution function $t^n$, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max_i U_i] = \int_0^1 (1 - t^n)\, dt = \frac{n}{n+1} .
$$
For $n$ independent exponential variables of mean 1, the gaps between consecutive order statistics are independent exponentials of means $1/n, 1/(n-1), \dots, 1$, so the expected maximum is the harmonic number $H_n \approx \ln n$.
:::

### 0.2 Independence of the future

An online algorithm decides at step $i$ with what it saw before. With independent values, “still active at step $i$” says nothing about $X_i$.

::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Independence of the future]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent and let $A$ be an event determined by $X_1, \dots, X_{i-1}$ and by an independent randomization. Then, for every integrable function $g$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[g(X_i)\, \mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}[g(X_i)]\; \mathbb{P}(A) .
$$
This is the definition of independence applied to $g(X_i)$ and $\mathbf{1}_A$; it is the single probabilistic step of the prophet inequalities of ch. 3.
:::

### 0.3 Linear programming and weak duality

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — Primal and dual programs]{.tag} For a matrix $A$ and vectors $b$, $c$, the primal and dual programs are
$$
(P)\ \max \{ c^\top x : A x \leq b,\ x \geq 0 \}, \qquad (D)\ \min \{ b^\top y : A^\top y \geq c,\ y \geq 0 \}.
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.6 — Weak and strong duality]{.tag} If $x$ is feasible for $(P)$ and $y$ is feasible for $(D)$, then
$$
c^\top x \leq b^\top y .
$$
If $(P)$ has a finite optimum, so does $(D)$, and the two optimal values are equal.

::: proof
Weak duality: $c^\top x \leq (A^\top y)^\top x = y^\top A x \leq y^\top b$, using $x \geq 0$, $y \geq 0$ and both sets of constraints. Strong duality follows from Farkas' lemma; see Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis (1997, ch. 4) or the [optimization refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Weak duality drives the **primal–dual method** of ch. 5 and 6: an online algorithm builds a primal solution and a dual one of value at most $c$ times larger. If the dual is feasible, it bounds the optimum, and the algorithm is $1/c$-competitive.

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Matching, vertex cover and their LPs]{.tag} In a graph $G = (V, E)$, a **matching** is a set of edges without common vertex. Its fractional relaxation and the dual, a fractional **vertex cover**, are
$$
\max \Big\{ \sum_{e} x_e : \sum_{e \ni v} x_e \leq 1\ \forall v,\ x \geq 0 \Big\}, \qquad \min \Big\{ \sum_v y_v : y_u + y_v \geq 1\ \forall uv \in E,\ y \geq 0 \Big\}.
$$
For bipartite graphs both programs have integral optima, and the maximum matching size equals the minimum vertex cover size (König's theorem).
:::

### 0.4 Maximal matchings and metric spaces

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Maximal matchings are half-optimal]{.tag} A matching $M$ to which no edge can be added satisfies
$$
|M| \geq \tfrac12\, |M^\star| \quad \text{for every matching } M^\star .
$$

::: proof
Every edge of $M^\star$ has an endpoint covered by $M$, otherwise it could be added. Each edge of $M$ covers two vertices, each of which belongs to at most one edge of $M^\star$. Hence $|M^\star| \leq 2|M|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A **metric space** $(X, d)$ is a set with a distance that is symmetric, zero exactly on the diagonal and satisfies the triangle inequality. The servers of ch. 8 and the requests of ch. 9 live in such spaces; the line, with $d(x, y) = |x - y|$, and the uniform metric, with all distances equal to 1, are the two running examples.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The expected maximum is at most a threshold plus the sum of the expected excesses over it (Proposition 0.2).
-   With independent values, being still active at step $i$ is independent of the value at step $i$.
-   Weak duality turns any feasible dual solution into an upper bound on the offline optimum.
-   A maximal matching has at least half the size of a maximum matching.
::::

## 1. Online algorithms and competitive analysis {#ch1}

An online algorithm receives its input one piece at a time and must answer each piece before seeing the next. This chapter defines how such an algorithm is judged, solves the simplest non-trivial example, ski rental, and gives the standard tool for lower bounds.

### 1.1 The online model

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Online problem]{.tag} An input is a sequence of requests $\sigma = (\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_T)$. An **online algorithm** chooses its decision for $\sigma_t$ knowing only $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_t$, and the decision cannot be undone. The **offline optimum** $\mathrm{OPT}(\sigma)$ is the best cost, or the best gain, achievable with the whole of $\sigma$ known in advance.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Competitive ratio]{.tag} For a cost minimization problem, an algorithm $\mathrm{ALG}$ is **$c$-competitive** if there is a constant $\alpha$ with, for every input $\sigma$,
$$
\mathrm{ALG}(\sigma) \leq c \cdot \mathrm{OPT}(\sigma) + \alpha .
$$
For a gain maximization problem, it is $c$-competitive, with $c \leq 1$, if $\mathrm{ALG}(\sigma) \geq c \cdot \mathrm{OPT}(\sigma)$ for every $\sigma$.

A randomized algorithm replaces $\mathrm{ALG}(\sigma)$ by its expectation over the coins of the algorithm. The input is fixed before the coins are tossed: this is the **oblivious adversary**.
:::

Ratios are above 1 for costs (paging, k-server) and below 1 for gains (prophets, matching). Against an adaptive adversary, who sees the coins as they fall, randomization brings nothing (Ben-David, Borodin, Karp, Tardos and Wigderson, 1994).

### 1.2 Ski rental

Renting skis costs 1 per day and buying them costs $B$ days of rent. The trip lasts $d$ days, unknown in advance, and the skier learns each morning whether the trip goes on. The offline optimum is
$$
\mathrm{OPT}(d) = \min(d, B).
$$

A deterministic algorithm is a day $k$ on which to buy if the trip is still going. It pays $d$ if $d < k$, and $k - 1 + B$ otherwise.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Deterministic ski rental]{.tag} Buying on day $B$ is $(2 - 1/B)$-competitive, and no deterministic algorithm has a smaller ratio.

::: proof
*Upper bound.* If $d < B$, the algorithm pays $d = \mathrm{OPT}$. If $d \geq B$, it pays $2B - 1$ while $\mathrm{OPT} = B$.

*Lower bound.* Against “buy on day $k$”, the adversary stops the trip right after the purchase, so $d = k$. The algorithm pays $k - 1 + B$ and $\mathrm{OPT} = \min(k, B)$.

-   If $k \leq B$, the ratio is $1 + (B - 1)/k \geq 2 - 1/B$.
-   If $k > B$, the ratio is $(k - 1 + B)/B \geq 2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Randomization helps. In continuous time, buy at a random time $t \in [0, B]$ with density
$$
p(t) = \frac{e^{t/B}}{B\,(e - 1)} .
$$
For a trip of length $d \leq B$, the expected cost is
$$
\int_0^d (t + B)\, p(t)\, dt + d \int_d^B p(t)\, dt = \frac{e}{e-1}\, d ,
$$
by an integration by parts, and for $d > B$ it is the value at $d = B$. The ratio $e/(e - 1) \approx 1.582$ is optimal (Karlin, Manasse, McGeoch and Owicki, 1994); the lower bound comes from the principle below.

### 1.3 Yao's principle

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Yao's principle for competitive ratios]{.tag} Let $D$ be a probability distribution on a finite set of inputs, and suppose that every deterministic algorithm $A$ satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim D}[A(\sigma)] \geq c\; \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim D}[\mathrm{OPT}(\sigma)] .
$$
Then every randomized algorithm $R$ has an input $\sigma$ with
$$
\mathbb{E}[R(\sigma)] \geq c \cdot \mathrm{OPT}(\sigma) .
$$

::: proof
A randomized algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic algorithms. By Fubini,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim D}\, \mathbb{E}_{A \sim R}[A(\sigma)] = \mathbb{E}_{A \sim R}\, \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim D}[A(\sigma)] \geq c\, \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim D}[\mathrm{OPT}(\sigma)] .
$$
The random variable $\mathbb{E}_R[R(\sigma)] - c\, \mathrm{OPT}(\sigma)$ therefore has a non-negative mean under $D$, so it is non-negative for at least one $\sigma$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A randomized lower bound thus only needs one distribution of hard inputs. Exercise 8 applies it to ski rental with $B = 2$, where the optimal randomized ratio is 4/3.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

B = 10                      # price of the skis, in days of rent
days = np.arange(1, B + 1)  # d >= B behaves like d = B (OPT = B)

def cost(k, d):             # buy on the morning of day k, ski for d days
    return d if d < k else (k - 1) + B

def opt(d):
    return min(d, B)

# Deterministic: worst-case ratio of "buy on day k"
for k in [1, 5, B, 15]:
    worst = max(cost(k, d) / opt(d) for d in range(1, 3 * B))
    print(f"buy on day {k:2d}: worst ratio {worst:.3f}")

# Randomized: the best distribution over k = 1..B solves an LP
# variables (p_1..p_B, c); minimise c s.t. E[cost(d)] <= c * opt(d) for all d
A, b = [], []
for d in days:
    A.append([cost(k, d) for k in days] + [-opt(d)])
    b.append(0.0)
res = linprog(c=[0] * B + [1], A_ub=A, b_ub=b,
              A_eq=[[1] * B + [0]], b_eq=[1], bounds=[(0, None)] * (B + 1), method="highs")
p, ratio = res.x[:B], res.x[B]
print("optimal randomized ratio:", round(ratio, 4))
print("closed form 1/(1-(1-1/B)^B):", round(1 / (1 - (1 - 1 / B) ** B), 4), " limit e/(e-1):", round(np.e / (np.e - 1), 4))
print("p_k ratios p_{k+1}/p_k:", np.round(p[1:] / p[:-1], 4)[:4])
```

With $B = 10$, buying on day 10 has worst ratio 1.900, while buying on day 1 or day 15 is far worse. The LP over distributions of the buying day returns 1.5353, the discrete form of $e/(e-1)$:
$$
\frac{1}{1 - (1 - 1/B)^B} = 1.5353 .
$$
The optimal probabilities grow geometrically, by the factor $1/(1 - 1/B)$ per day, the discrete twin of the density $p(t)$.

### 1.4 Online algorithms are not online learning

The course description insists on a disclaimer: online algorithms are related to online learning and bandits, but the question is *when* to make a decision rather than *which* decision to make.

-   **Online learning** repeats the same decision problem. The benchmark is the best *fixed* action in hindsight, decisions do not change future problems, and regret grows sublinearly (see [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html)).
-   **Online algorithms** carry a state: a budget spent, a vertex matched, a server position. The benchmark is the best *sequence* of decisions in hindsight, with a multiplicative guarantee on every input.

In ski rental there is no fixed action to learn: the whole problem is one decision of when to buy. Bridges exist all the same, and ch. 6.3 and ch. 8.4 use online convex optimization inside online algorithms.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   An online algorithm is judged by its competitive ratio against the offline optimum, on every input.
-   Randomized algorithms are judged against an oblivious adversary, who fixes the input before the coins are tossed.
-   Ski rental: buying on day $B$ gives $2 - 1/B$ deterministically; randomization gives $e/(e-1)$, and both are optimal.
-   Yao's principle turns a distribution of hard inputs into a lower bound for randomized algorithms.
-   Competitive analysis compares with the best sequence of decisions; online learning compares with the best fixed action.
::::

## 2. Stopping times and the secretary problem {#ch2}

A stopping problem asks for the best moment to take an irrevocable action while information keeps arriving. This chapter solves it by backward induction and applies the method to the secretary problem.

### 2.1 Filtrations and stopping times

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Filtration and stopping time]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be the observations and $\mathcal{F}_t = \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_t)$ the information available at time $t$. A random time $\tau$ with values in $\{1, \dots, n\} \cup \{\infty\}$ is a **stopping time** if, for every $t$,
$$
\{\tau = t\} \in \mathcal{F}_t .
$$
The decision to stop at $t$ uses the past and the present, never the future. A **randomized** stopping time may also use a random variable drawn at the start, independent of the observations.
:::

The first time $X_t$ exceeds a fixed threshold is a stopping time. The time of the overall maximum is not, since recognizing it requires later values; the prophet of ch. 3 is the player allowed to use it.

### 2.2 Backward induction

Let $Y_t$ be the reward for stopping at time $t$, a function of $X_1, \dots, X_t$, with $\mathbb{E}|Y_t| < \infty$. The problem is to maximize $\mathbb{E}[Y_\tau]$ over stopping times $\tau \leq n$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Snell envelope]{.tag} Define backwards $V_n = Y_n$ and
$$
V_t = \max\big(Y_t,\ \mathbb{E}[V_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]\big), \qquad t = n-1, \dots, 1.
$$
The stopping time $\tau^\star = \min\{t : Y_t = V_t\}$ is optimal, and
$$
\max_{\tau} \mathbb{E}[Y_\tau] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{\tau^\star}] = \mathbb{E}[V_1].
$$

::: proof
1.  For any stopping time $\tau \leq n$, write the telescoping sum
    $$
    V_\tau = V_1 + \sum_{t=1}^{n-1} (V_{t+1} - V_t)\, \mathbf{1}\{\tau > t\} .
    $$
2.  The event $\{\tau > t\}$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_t$, and $\mathbb{E}[V_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] \leq V_t$ by definition. Each term has a non-positive expectation, so $\mathbb{E}[V_\tau] \leq \mathbb{E}[V_1]$.
3.  Since $Y_\tau \leq V_\tau$, every stopping time gives $\mathbb{E}[Y_\tau] \leq \mathbb{E}[V_1]$.
4.  For $\tau^\star$, on $\{\tau^\star > t\}$ we have $Y_t < V_t$, hence $V_t = \mathbb{E}[V_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$. Every term of step 2 has zero expectation, and $Y_{\tau^\star} = V_{\tau^\star}$, so equality holds. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The process $(V_t)$, the **Snell envelope**, is the smallest supermartingale above $(Y_t)$.

When the $X_t$ are independent and $Y_t = X_t$, the conditional expectations are constants. With $v_{n+1} = 0$, the values satisfy
$$
v_t = \mathbb{E}\big[\max(X_t,\ v_{t+1})\big],
$$
and the optimal rule stops at the first $t$ with $X_t \geq v_{t+1}$, a sequence of decreasing thresholds.

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — Three uniform offers]{.tag} Three independent offers, uniform on $[0, 1]$, arrive in turn.

-   At the last step, $v_3 = 1/2$.
-   Then $v_2 = \mathbb{E}[\max(U, 1/2)] = 5/8$: accept the second offer if it exceeds 1/2.
-   Then $v_1 = \mathbb{E}[\max(U, 5/8)] = 89/128$: accept the first offer if it exceeds 5/8.

The optimal value is
$$
v_1 = 89/128 \approx 0.695,
$$
against $\mathbb{E}[\max] = 3/4$ for a player who sees all three offers (Example 0.3).
:::

### 2.3 The secretary problem

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Secretary problem]{.tag} Candidates $1, \dots, n$ have distinct qualities and arrive in a uniformly random order. After each interview, the employer knows only how the current candidate compares with those already seen, and hires or rejects for good. The goal is to maximize the probability of hiring the best candidate.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — The 1/e law (Lindley, 1961; Dynkin, 1963)]{.tag} The rule that rejects the first $r - 1$ candidates and then hires the first one better than all before succeeds with probability
$$
P_n(r) = \frac{r-1}{n} \sum_{i=r}^{n} \frac{1}{i-1} \qquad (2 \leq r \leq n).
$$
The best $r$ satisfies $r/n \to 1/e$, and

::: key
[Key result — the 1/e law]{.tag}
$$
\max_r P_n(r) \longrightarrow \frac1e \approx 0.368 .
$$
:::

::: proof
1.  The best candidate is at position $i$ with probability $1/n$.
2.  The rule hires it if and only if $i \geq r$ and nobody before position $i$ triggers the rule first.
3.  That happens exactly when the best of the first $i - 1$ candidates sits among the first $r - 1$, an event of probability $(r-1)/(i-1)$.
4.  Summing over $i$ gives $P_n(r)$.
5.  With $r \approx xn$, the sum is a Riemann sum, and
    $$
    P_n(r) \to x \int_x^1 \frac{dt}{t} = -x \ln x ,
    $$
    maximal at $x = 1/e$ with value $1/e$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The threshold rule is optimal among all stopping rules. Call candidate $i$ a **record** if it beats everybody before it; the indicators of records are independent, with probabilities $1/i$ (Rényi). A record at position $i$ is the overall best with probability $i/n$, increasing in $i$, while the value of continuing decreases, so backward induction stops at the first record after a fixed position.

The same structure solves a larger family. Bruss's **odds theorem** (2000) considers independent events $I_1, \dots, I_n$ of probabilities $p_j$ and odds $r_j = p_j / (1 - p_j)$, and the goal of stopping on the last event that occurs. The optimal rule stops at the first event from index $s$ on, where $s$ is the largest index with
$$
\sum_{j \geq s} r_j \geq 1 .
$$
It wins exactly when one event occurs among $I_s, \dots, I_n$, with probability $\prod_{j \geq s}(1 - p_j) \sum_{j \geq s} r_j$, and this probability is at least $1/e$ whenever the total odds reach 1 (Bruss, 2003). Records give $p_j = 1/j$ and recover Theorem 2.5.

### 2.4 The secretary problem as a linear program

Buchbinder, Jain and Singh (2014) write every stopping rule as a point of a polytope. Let $x_i$ be the probability that a rule hires the candidate at position $i$. Hiring candidate $i$ requires that nobody was hired before and that $i$ is a record, two independent events, so
$$
x_i \leq \frac{1}{i} \Big(1 - \sum_{j < i} x_j\Big).
$$
A rule that only hires records wins with probability $\sum_i (i/n)\, x_i$. Conversely, every feasible $x$ is realized by the rule that hires a record at position $i$ with the right conditional probability.

::: thm
[Proposition 2.6 — The secretary LP]{.tag} The best success probability equals the value of
$$
\max \Big\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i}{n}\, x_i \ :\ i\, x_i + \sum_{j < i} x_j \leq 1\ \ \forall i,\ \ x \geq 0 \Big\}.
$$
Its optimal solution is $x_i = 0$ before the threshold and $x_i = (r - 1)/(i(i-1))$ from $r$ on, the threshold rule; a dual solution certifies its optimality.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

n = 100

def success(r, n):          # reject the first r-1, then take the first record
    if r == 1:
        return 1 / n
    return (r - 1) / n * sum(1 / (i - 1) for i in range(r, n + 1))

r_star = max(range(1, n + 1), key=lambda r: success(r, n))
print(f"n={n}: best r = {r_star}, P(best) = {success(r_star, n):.4f}, 1/e = {1/np.e:.4f}")

# The LP of Buchbinder, Jain and Singh: x_i = P(select the i-th candidate)
#   max sum_i (i/n) x_i   s.t.   i * x_i + sum_{j<i} x_j <= 1,  x >= 0
A = np.tril(np.ones((n, n)), -1) + np.diag(np.arange(1, n + 1))
res = linprog(-np.arange(1, n + 1) / n, A_ub=A, b_ub=np.ones(n),
              bounds=[(0, None)] * n, method="highs")
x = res.x
print(f"LP value = {-res.fun:.4f}; first index with x_i > 0: {np.argmax(x > 1e-9) + 1}")

# Monte Carlo check of the threshold rule
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
trials, wins = 100_000, 0
for _ in range(trials):
    ranks = rng.permutation(n)          # rank 0 = best candidate
    best_seen = ranks[: r_star - 1].min()
    later = ranks[r_star - 1:]
    pick = later[np.argmax(later < best_seen)] if (later < best_seen).any() else None
    wins += (pick == 0)
print(f"simulated success: {wins / trials:.4f}")
```

For $n = 100$, the best rule rejects the first 37 candidates and wins with probability 0.3710, slightly above $1/e$. The LP returns the same value, positive from position 38 on, and 100,000 simulated orders give 0.3703.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   A stopping time decides with the past and present only; the time of the maximum is not one.
-   Backward induction (the Snell envelope) solves every finite-horizon stopping problem.
-   With independent values, the optimal rule uses decreasing thresholds $v_{t+1}$.
-   The secretary problem: skip about $n/e$ candidates, then take the first record; success tends to $1/e$.
-   The odds theorem and the secretary LP generalize the 1/e law.
::::

## 3. Prophet inequalities {#ch3}

A gambler sees independent values one at a time and may stop once; a prophet sees them all and takes the largest. This chapter shows that a stopping rule secures half of the prophet's expected gain in general, and $1 - 1/e$ for identically distributed values.

### 3.1 The gambler and the prophet

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Prophet inequality setting]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent, non-negative and integrable, with known distributions, observed in this order. The gambler chooses a (possibly randomized) stopping time $\tau$ and receives $X_\tau$, or 0 if he never stops. The prophet receives $\max_i X_i$. The competitive ratio of a rule is the worst case, over all distributions, of
$$
\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_\tau]}{\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]} .
$$
:::

The course description writes the ratio as $\mathbb{E}[X_\tau] / \max_i X_i$; the standard benchmark is the expectation of the maximum. Backward induction (Theorem 2.2) gives the optimal gambler, but its value is hard to compare with the prophet. **Threshold rules**, which stop at the first $X_i \geq T$, are easier to analyse and nearly as good.

### 3.2 The factor one half

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Prophet inequality (Krengel and Sucheston, 1977; Samuel-Cahn, 1984)]{.tag} Let $\tau$ stop at the first $X_i \geq T$, and let $p$ be the probability that it stops at all. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}[X_\tau] \geq p\, T + (1 - p)\, \big(\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i] - T\big).
$$
With $T = \mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]/2$ (Kleinberg and Weinberg, 2012), or with $T$ chosen so that $p = 1/2$ (Samuel-Cahn, 1984),

::: key
[Key result — the prophet inequality]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}[X_\tau] \geq \tfrac12\, \mathbb{E}\big[\max_i X_i\big].
$$
:::

::: proof
1.  Split the gain into the threshold and the excess over it. When the rule stops at $i$, $X_i = T + (X_i - T)^+$, so
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[X_\tau] = p\, T + \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\big[(X_i - T)^+\, \mathbf{1}\{\tau \geq i\}\big].
    $$
2.  The event $\{\tau \geq i\}$, that no earlier value reached $T$, depends on $X_1, \dots, X_{i-1}$ only. By Proposition 0.4 the $i$-th term is $\mathbb{E}[(X_i - T)^+]\, \mathbb{P}(\tau \geq i)$.
3.  Each $\mathbb{P}(\tau \geq i)$ is at least the probability $1 - p$ of never stopping.
4.  By Proposition 0.2, the sum of the expected excesses is at least $\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i] - T$. This gives the first inequality.
5.  With $T = \mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]/2$, both terms carry the factor $T$ and add up to $T$. With $p = 1/2$, the right side is $T/2 + (\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i] - T)/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The rule with $T = \mathbb{E}[\max]/2$ needs only one number about the distributions, a robustness that matters for the auctions of ch. 4.

::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — The factor 1/2 is tight]{.tag} No stopping rule, even the optimal one, guarantees more than $1/2$. Take $n = 2$, $X_1 = 1$, and $X_2 = 1/\varepsilon$ with probability $\varepsilon$, 0 otherwise. The prophet gets
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max(X_1, X_2)] = (1 - \varepsilon) + 1 = 2 - \varepsilon .
$$
The gambler gets 1 whether he stops at $X_1$ or waits, since $\mathbb{E}[X_2] = 1$. The ratio $1/(2 - \varepsilon)$ tends to $1/2$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Three uniform offers again]{.tag} For the offers of Example 2.3, $\mathbb{E}[\max] = 3/4$ and the optimal gambler gets $0.695$, a ratio of 0.927. The threshold $T = 3/8$ stops at the first offer above it:
$$
\mathbb{E}[X_\tau] = \frac{1 - T^2}{2}\,(1 + T + T^2) = \frac{55}{128} \cdot \frac{97}{64} \approx 0.651,
$$
a ratio of 0.868, well above the guarantee of 1/2. The median threshold $2^{-1/3} \approx 0.794$ is too demanding here and gets only 0.598 of the prophet.
:::

### 3.3 Identically distributed values

For i.i.d. values, a single threshold already does better than 1/2.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.5 — The i.i.d. prophet inequality with one threshold]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with a continuous distribution, and let $T$ satisfy $\mathbb{P}(X_1 \geq T) = 1/n$. The threshold rule satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}[X_\tau] \geq \Big(1 - \big(1 - \tfrac1n\big)^n\Big)\, \mathbb{E}\big[\max_i X_i\big] \geq \Big(1 - \frac1e\Big)\, \mathbb{E}\big[\max_i X_i\big].
$$

::: proof
1.  Write $q = 1/n$ and $p = 1 - (1 - q)^n$ for the probability of stopping. Step 1 of Theorem 3.2 with $\mathbb{P}(\tau \geq i) = (1 - q)^{i-1}$ gives
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[X_\tau] = p\, T + \mathbb{E}[(X_1 - T)^+] \sum_{i=1}^n (1 - q)^{i-1} = p \Big(T + \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_1 - T)^+]}{q}\Big).
    $$
2.  Since $1/q = n$, the bracket is $T + n\, \mathbb{E}[(X_1 - T)^+]$, which is at least $\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$ by Proposition 0.2.
3.  Finally $(1 - 1/n)^n \leq 1/e$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Adaptive thresholds do even better in the i.i.d. case. Hill and Kertz (1982) began the study of the optimal i.i.d. constant, Kertz (1986) identified the candidate value $\approx 0.745$, and Correa, Foncea, Hoeksma, Oosterwijk and Vredeveld (2017) proved that it is the exact worst-case ratio of the optimal gambler.

### 3.4 Random order: the prophet secretary

In the **prophet secretary**, the distributions differ but the values arrive in a uniformly random order. Esfandiari, Hajiaghayi, Liaghat and Monemizadeh (2015) reached $1 - 1/e$ with decreasing thresholds, and Correa, Saona and Ziliotto (2019) went beyond it with “blind” strategies. The optimal constant is open, as in the **free order** model, where the gambler chooses the order.

### 3.5 The ex-ante relaxation and contention resolution

The linear-optimisation view of ch. 2.4 also bounds the prophet. Let $x_i$ be the probability that the prophet takes $X_i$, so that $\sum_i x_i \leq 1$.

Among all events of probability $x_i$, the one that maximizes the expected gain from $X_i$ is “$X_i$ lies in its top $x_i$-quantile”; call $r_i(x_i)$ that gain. This gives the **ex-ante relaxation**:
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\max_i X_i\big] \leq \max \Big\{ \sum_{i=1}^n r_i(x_i) : \sum_i x_i \leq 1,\ x \geq 0 \Big\}.
$$

An online algorithm then tries to select each $i$ with probability close to $x_i$. Call $i$ **active** if $X_i$ falls in its top $x_i$-quantile.

:::: thm
[Proposition 3.6 — A 1/2 online contention resolution scheme]{.tag} If nothing has been selected before step $i$ and $i$ is active, select it with probability
$$
\frac{1}{2\,\big(1 - \sum_{j<i} x_j/2\big)} .
$$
Then each $i$ is selected with probability exactly $x_i/2$, and the expected gain is half the value of the ex-ante relaxation, hence at least $\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]/2$.

::: proof
1.  By induction, nothing is selected before $i$ with probability $1 - \sum_{j<i} x_j/2 \geq 1/2$, so the selection probability above is at most 1.
2.  Activity of $i$ is independent of the past (Proposition 0.4). Multiplying the three probabilities gives $x_i/2$.
3.  The decision does not depend on where $X_i$ lies inside its top quantile, so the gain from $i$ is $r_i(x_i)/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Feldman, Svensson and Zenklusen (2016) extend contention resolution to matroids, matchings and knapsacks, the route to prophet inequalities for many items.

```python
import numpy as np

n = 3                        # X_1, X_2, X_3 i.i.d. uniform on [0, 1]
E_max = n / (n + 1)

# Optimal gambler (backward induction of ch. 2.2): v_n = 1/2, v_t = E[max(U, v_{t+1})]
v = 0.5
for _ in range(n - 1):
    v = (1 + v ** 2) / 2
print(f"prophet E[max] = {E_max:.4f}, optimal gambler = {v:.4f}, ratio {v / E_max:.3f}")

def threshold_value(T):      # E[X_tau] for 'stop at the first X_i >= T'
    return (1 - T ** 2) / 2 * sum(T ** i for i in range(n))

rules = {"T = E[max]/2": E_max / 2,
         "median of max": 0.5 ** (1 / n),
         "P(X >= T) = 1/n": 1 - 1 / n}
Ts = np.linspace(0, 1, 100_001)
rules["best single T"] = Ts[np.argmax(threshold_value(Ts))]
for name, T in rules.items():
    print(f"{name:16s} T = {T:.4f}  E[X_tau] = {threshold_value(T):.4f}  ratio {threshold_value(T) / E_max:.3f}")

# Ex-ante LP + online contention resolution scheme (OCRS), by simulation
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = np.full(n, 1 / n)                       # LP solution (symmetric)
LP = n * (x[0] - x[0] ** 2 / 2)             # sum_i E[X_i ; X_i >= 1 - x_i]
X = rng.random((200_000, n))
gain = np.zeros(len(X))
free = np.ones(len(X), dtype=bool)
for i in range(n):
    active = X[:, i] >= 1 - x[i]
    accept = rng.random(len(X)) < 1 / (2 * (1 - x[:i].sum() / 2))
    take = free & active & accept
    gain[take] = X[take, i]
    free &= ~take
print(f"ex-ante LP = {LP:.4f} >= E[max]; OCRS value = {gain.mean():.4f} (LP/2 = {LP / 2:.4f})")
```

The run confirms Example 3.4. The $1/n$-quantile threshold of Theorem 3.5 gets 0.782 of the prophet, above its guarantee 0.704, and the best single threshold, $T \approx 0.455$, gets 0.879. The ex-ante LP is worth $5/6$, and contention resolution collects half of it, 0.416: weak here, but robust to combinatorial constraints.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Prophet inequality: one threshold, $T = \mathbb{E}[\max]/2$ or the median of the maximum, secures half the prophet's gain.
-   The proof splits the gain into threshold and excess and uses only independence and Proposition 0.2.
-   The factor 1/2 is tight, already with two values.
-   For i.i.d. values, the $1/n$-quantile threshold gives $1 - 1/e$, and adaptive thresholds reach about 0.745.
-   The ex-ante LP bounds the prophet; online contention resolution rounds it with a factor 1/2.
::::

## 4. Pandora's box, posted prices and online auctions {#ch4}

In Pandora's problem, the decision maker chooses which value to inspect next and pays for each inspection. This chapter derives the optimal policy, then turns stopping rules into prices, the modern motivation of prophet inequalities.

### 4.1 Pandora's box

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Pandora's problem and reservation values]{.tag} Box $i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ contains an independent value $V_i \geq 0$ with known distribution, and opening it costs $c_i > 0$. Boxes are opened one at a time in an adaptive order; at any moment Pandora may stop and keep the largest value found. Her utility is that value minus the total cost paid. The **reservation value** $\sigma_i$ of box $i$ solves
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(V_i - \sigma_i)^+\big] = c_i .
$$
:::

The reservation value is the price at which Pandora is indifferent between holding a sure value $\sigma_i$ and paying $c_i$ to see whether the box beats it.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Weitzman's rule (Weitzman, 1979)]{.tag} The following policy is optimal: open the boxes in decreasing order of $\sigma_i$, and stop as soon as the best value found is at least the largest reservation value among the closed boxes. Its expected utility is
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_i \kappa_i\Big], \qquad \kappa_i = \min(V_i, \sigma_i).
$$

::: proof
The proof of Kleinberg, Waggoner and Weyl (2016) compares every policy with the **capped values** $\kappa_i$. Let $I_i$ indicate that box $i$ is opened and $A_i \leq I_i$ that its value is kept.

1.  The decision to open box $i$ is taken before seeing $V_i$, so $I_i$ is independent of $V_i$ and
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[I_i\, c_i] = \mathbb{E}\big[I_i\, (V_i - \sigma_i)^+\big].
    $$
2.  Hence the utility of any policy satisfies
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i A_i V_i - I_i c_i\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i A_i V_i - I_i (V_i - \sigma_i)^+\Big] \leq \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i A_i \kappa_i\Big],
    $$
    using $A_i \leq I_i$ and $V_i - (V_i - \sigma_i)^+ = \kappa_i$.
3.  At most one box is kept, so the right side is at most $\mathbb{E}[\max_i \kappa_i]$, for every policy.
4.  Step 2 is an equality when every opened box with $V_i > \sigma_i$ is kept. Under Weitzman's rule, such a box beats every remaining reservation value, and the best value seen before it, which was below $\sigma_i$; the rule stops at once and keeps it.
5.  Step 3 is an equality when the kept box $s$ has the largest capped value. If $V_s \leq \sigma_s$, then $\kappa_s = V_s$ dominates the values opened and the reservation values left. Otherwise $s$ was kept right after being opened, and every other $\kappa_j$ lies below $\sigma_s = \kappa_s$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Two boxes]{.tag} Box 1 holds a uniform value on $[0, 1]$ and costs 0.08; box 2 holds 2 or 0 with probability 1/2 each and costs 0.4.

-   Box 1: $(1 - \sigma_1)^2/2 = 0.08$ gives $\sigma_1 = 0.6$. Box 2: $(2 - \sigma_2)/2 = 0.4$ gives $\sigma_2 = 1.2$.
-   Open box 2 first. If it holds 2, stop, since $2 \geq 0.6$. Otherwise open box 1 and keep its value.
-   The utility is $-0.4 + 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.5\,(0.5 - 0.08)$, and the capped values give the same number:
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max(\kappa_1, \kappa_2)] = 0.5 \cdot 1.2 + 0.5 \cdot 0.42 = 0.81 .
$$
Opening box 1 first is worse: box 1 never reveals more than $\sigma_2$, so box 2 is always opened, and the utility drops to 0.77.
:::

The reservation value of a box depends on that box only. Variants break this: when Pandora may take a box without opening it (Doval, 2018; Beyhaghi and Kleinberg, 2019), index-based policies only approximate the optimum.

### 4.2 From stopping rules to posted prices

A seller has one item and buyers arrive one by one, with independent private values $V_i \sim F_i$. The seller posts a price $p_i$ to buyer $i$, who buys if $V_i \geq p_i$. One price $T$ for everybody is the threshold rule of ch. 3, seen from the buyers' side.

-   **Welfare.** By Theorem 3.2, the price $T = \mathbb{E}[\max_i V_i]/2$ gives the item to a buyer worth at least half the best one in expectation, the welfare of an auction with all buyers present (Hajiaghayi, Kleinberg and Sandholm, 2007).
-   **Simplicity.** Each buyer faces a take-it-or-leave-it offer, so truth-telling is trivial and buyers need not be present together (Lucier, 2017).

### 4.3 Revenue and virtual values

For revenue, Myerson's theory supplies the right variables. Let $F_i$ have a density $f_i$ and define the **virtual value**
$$
\varphi_i(v) = v - \frac{1 - F_i(v)}{f_i(v)} .
$$
The distribution is **regular** if $\varphi_i$ is non-decreasing.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Myerson's lemma (Myerson, 1981)]{.tag} For every truthful mechanism, the expected revenue equals the expected virtual value of the winner. Consequently, for regular distributions, the optimal auction gives the item to the buyer with the largest virtual value when it is non-negative, and its revenue is
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_i\, \varphi_i(V_i)^+\Big].
$$
:::

Apply the prophet inequality to the independent variables $\varphi_i(V_i)^+$. A threshold $T$ on virtual values is the price $\varphi_i^{-1}(T)$ for buyer $i$, and its revenue is the virtual value it collects. Chawla, Hartline, Malec and Sivan (2010) deduce that sequential posted prices earn half the optimal revenue, and extend this to several items.

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — Two uniform buyers]{.tag} With two buyers uniform on $[0, 1]$, $\varphi(v) = 2v - 1$. The optimal auction is a second-price auction with reserve price 1/2, and its revenue is $5/12 \approx 0.417$.

-   One price $p$ for both buyers earns $p\,(1 - p^2)$, maximal at $p = 1/\sqrt{3}$ with $0.385$.
-   Adapted prices, $p_1$ for the first buyer and then the single-buyer optimum 1/2 for the second, earn $p_1 (1 - p_1) + p_1/4$, maximal at $p_1 = 5/8$:
$$
\text{revenue} = 25/64 \approx 0.391,
$$
that is 94 % of the optimal auction, from prices computed by backward induction (Theorem 2.2).
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
N = 400_000
# Box 1: V ~ U[0,1], cost 0.08.  Box 2: V = 2 w.p. 1/2, else 0, cost 0.4.
samplers = [lambda m: rng.random(m), lambda m: 2.0 * (rng.random(m) < 0.5)]
costs = np.array([0.08, 0.4])
excess = [lambda s: max(1 - s, 0) ** 2 / 2, lambda s: 0.5 * max(2 - s, 0)]   # E[(V - s)^+]
sigma = np.array([brentq(lambda s, i=i: excess[i](s) - costs[i], 0, 2) for i in range(2)])
print("reservation values sigma =", np.round(sigma, 4))

V = np.column_stack([f(N) for f in samplers])

def run(order):              # open in 'order', stop when best >= max remaining sigma
    best, paid = np.zeros(N), np.zeros(N)
    stopped = np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
    for j, i in enumerate(order):
        rest = sigma[order[j:]].max()
        stopped |= best >= rest
        go = ~stopped
        paid[go] += costs[i]
        best[go] = np.maximum(best[go], V[go, i])
    return (best - paid).mean()

print(f"Weitzman order {np.argsort(-sigma) + 1}: utility {run(np.argsort(-sigma)):.4f}")
print(f"reverse order: utility {run(np.argsort(sigma)):.4f}")
kappa = np.minimum(V, sigma)
print(f"E[max capped value] = {kappa.max(axis=1).mean():.4f}")

# Posted prices for one item and two buyers with values U[0,1]
p = np.linspace(0, 1, 100_001)
single = p * (1 - p ** 2)                          # same price for both buyers
adaptive = p * (1 - p) + p * 0.25                  # price p, then 1/2 to buyer 2
print(f"one price: best p = {p[single.argmax()]:.4f}, revenue {single.max():.4f}")
print(f"two prices: best p1 = {p[adaptive.argmax()]:.4f}, revenue {adaptive.max():.4f}")
print(f"Myerson optimal auction revenue = {5 / 12:.4f}")
```

The simulation recovers the reservation values 0.6 and 1.2, a utility of 0.809 for Weitzman's order against 0.769 for the reverse order, and $\mathbb{E}[\max_i \kappa_i] = 0.810$; the pricing part reproduces Example 4.5.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   The reservation value of a box solves $\mathbb{E}[(V - \sigma)^+] = c$ and depends on that box only.
-   Weitzman's rule, by decreasing reservation values with a stopping test, is optimal, and its value is the expected maximum capped value.
-   A threshold stopping rule is a posted price; the prophet inequality makes one price half-optimal for welfare.
-   With Myerson's virtual values, the same argument makes sequential posted prices half-optimal for revenue.
::::

## 5. Online bipartite matching {#ch5}

In online matching, one side of a bipartite graph is known and the other arrives vertex by vertex, each matched at once or never. Deterministic algorithms lose half of the optimum; one random permutation recovers $1 - 1/e$.

### 5.1 The model

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Online bipartite matching]{.tag} Let $G = (U \cup V, E)$ be bipartite. The **offline** vertices $U$ are present from the start; the **online** vertices of $V$ arrive one at a time, each revealing its edges to $U$.

On arrival, an online vertex is matched to a still unmatched neighbour or left unmatched, irrevocably. The gain is the size of the final matching, compared with the maximum matching $\mathrm{OPT}$ of $G$.
:::

In advertising, offline vertices are advertisers, online vertices are queries, and an edge means the ad is relevant.

### 5.2 Greedy and its limit

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Greedy is 1/2-competitive, and no deterministic algorithm is better]{.tag} An algorithm that matches $v$ whenever $v$ has a free neighbour builds a maximal matching, hence $|M| \geq \mathrm{OPT}/2$ by Proposition 0.8.

Conversely, let $U = \{u_1, u_2\}$ and let the first online vertex be adjacent to both. A deterministic algorithm matches it to some $u$, or not at all. The adversary then sends a second online vertex adjacent only to that $u$. The algorithm ends with 1 edge while $\mathrm{OPT} = 2$.
:::

A uniformly random free neighbour does not fix this: on some graphs that rule matches only about half of the optimum (Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani, 1990).

### 5.3 RANKING

**RANKING** (Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani, 1990) draws one random order of $U$ at the start and matches every arriving vertex to its free neighbour of highest priority. Equivalently, each $u \in U$ draws $y_u$ uniform on $[0, 1]$, independently, and smaller $y_u$ means higher priority.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — RANKING is $(1 - 1/e)$-competitive]{.tag} For every bipartite graph and every arrival order,

::: key
[Key result — RANKING]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[|M_{\text{RANKING}}|\big] \geq \Big(1 - \frac1e\Big)\, \mathrm{OPT} .
$$
:::

::: proof
The randomized primal–dual proof of Devanur, Jain and Kleinberg (2013) builds dual variables while RANKING runs. Let $g(y) = e^{y - 1}$. When an online vertex $v$ is matched to $u$, set
$$
\alpha_u = g(y_u), \qquad \beta_v = 1 - g(y_u),
$$
and leave all other variables at 0. Each matched edge contributes exactly 1 to the dual objective, which therefore equals $|M|$.

1.  *Goal.* Suppose every edge $uv$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\alpha_u + \beta_v] \geq 1 - 1/e$. Then the expected duals, divided by $1 - 1/e$, form a fractional vertex cover of value $\mathbb{E}|M| / (1 - 1/e)$, and weak duality (Definition 0.7) bounds $\mathrm{OPT}$ by that value.
2.  *Freeze all but one value.* Fix an edge $uv$ and the values of all offline vertices other than $u$. Run RANKING on the graph without $u$, and call $y^c$ the value of the vertex that $v$ gets in that run, or 1 if it stays unmatched.
3.  *Monotonicity.* Adding $u$ back changes the run along a single alternating path, and every online vertex ends matched to a vertex of value at most its value without $u$ (a lemma of the same paper). Hence $\beta_v \geq 1 - g(y^c)$, whatever $y_u$.
4.  *Dominance.* If $y_u < y^c$, then $u$ ends up matched. Otherwise the run with $u$ never uses it and coincides with the run without it. But then, when $v$ arrives, $u$ is a free neighbour that beats the vertex $v$ picks in that run: a contradiction.
5.  *Integrate over $y_u$.* Steps 3 and 4 give
    $$
    \mathbb{E}_{y_u}[\alpha_u + \beta_v] \geq \int_0^{y^c} e^{y - 1}\, dy + 1 - e^{y^c - 1} = 1 - \frac1e .
    $$
    Averaging over the frozen values proves the goal of step 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — No online algorithm beats $1 - 1/e$]{.tag} Take $|U| = |V| = n$ and let $v_j$ be adjacent to $u_{\pi(j)}, \dots, u_{\pi(n)}$ for a hidden uniform relabelling $\pi$; the graph has a perfect matching. Whatever an algorithm does, the free offline vertices it sees are exchangeable, and the expected size of its matching is at most $(1 - 1/e)\, n + o(n)$. With Yao's principle (Theorem 1.4), the bound holds for randomized algorithms (Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani, 1990).
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, h, trials = 200, 100, 200

def trap():
    """v_i ~ u_i for all i; the first h online vertices also see u_h, ..., u_{n-1}."""
    return [np.r_[i, np.arange(h, n)] if i < h else np.array([i]) for i in range(n)]

def upper_triangular():
    """v_j sees u_pi(j), ..., u_pi(n-1) for a hidden random relabelling pi."""
    pi = rng.permutation(n)
    return [pi[j:] for j in range(n)]

def run(neigh, rule):
    rank = rng.permutation(n)          # used by RANKING only, drawn once
    matched, size = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool), 0
    for nb in neigh:                   # online vertices arrive one by one
        free = nb[~matched[nb]]
        if len(free) == 0:
            continue
        if rule == "greedy":           # a deterministic greedy rule
            u = free.max()
        elif rule == "random":         # uniformly random free neighbour
            u = rng.choice(free)
        else:                          # RANKING: smallest rank
            u = free[np.argmin(rank[free])]
        matched[u], size = True, size + 1
    return size

for name, make in [("trap", trap), ("upper triangular", upper_triangular)]:
    res = {r: np.mean([run(make(), r) for _ in range(trials)]) / n
           for r in ["greedy", "random", "ranking"]}
    print(f"{name:17s}", "  ".join(f"{r} {v:.3f}" for r, v in res.items()))
print(f"1 - 1/e = {1 - 1 / np.e:.3f}")
```

On the trap, early vertices may take shared vertices that late vertices need. Greedy, which prefers them, matches 0.500 of the optimum and the random rule 0.517, while RANKING reaches 0.684. On the graph of Proposition 5.4, all three are stuck at 0.633, the bound $1 - 1/e$ up to finite-size effects.

### 5.4 Beyond the adversary

The bound $1 - 1/e$ is a worst case over both the graph and the arrival order. Weaker adversaries allow more.

-   **Random order.** Goel and Mehta (2008) show that greedy is $(1 - 1/e)$-competitive when the online vertices arrive in random order, and Mahdian and Yan (2011) show that RANKING then reaches at least 0.696.
-   **Known i.i.d. arrivals.** When online vertices are drawn from a known distribution, Feldman, Mehta, Mirrokni and Muthukrishnan (2009) beat $1 - 1/e$ by planning on an offline sample.
-   **Open questions.** The exact random-order ratio of RANKING, and the best ratios when both sides arrive online, are open (ch. 10).

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Online bipartite matching: one side known, the other arriving with its edges; decisions are irrevocable.
-   Every greedy rule is 1/2-competitive, and no deterministic algorithm does better.
-   RANKING, one random priority order drawn in advance, is $(1 - 1/e)$-competitive, and no online algorithm does better.
-   The randomized primal–dual proof splits each matched edge between its endpoints with $g(y) = e^{y-1}$.
-   Random order and stochastic arrivals allow ratios above $1 - 1/e$.
::::

## 6. Budgets: b-matching, AdWords, resource allocation and delays {#ch6}

In advertising, an offline vertex is an advertiser matched many times until a budget runs out: spending now leaves less for later. This chapter extends ch. 5 to capacities and bids, then studies learned prices and matching with delays.

### 6.1 b-matching and BALANCE

In **b-matching**, each offline vertex can be matched up to $b$ times. Greedy is still 1/2-competitive (Exercise 10). **BALANCE** matches each arriving vertex to the neighbour that has used the smallest fraction of its capacity.

::: thm
[Theorem 6.1 — BALANCE (Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs, 2000)]{.tag} BALANCE is deterministic and
$$
1 - \frac{1}{(1 + 1/b)^b}\text{-competitive},
$$
a ratio that tends to $1 - 1/e$ as $b \to \infty$. No deterministic algorithm does better.
:::

Large capacities let a deterministic algorithm match what RANKING achieves with randomness for $b = 1$.

### 6.2 AdWords

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — AdWords]{.tag} Advertisers $u$ have budgets $B_u$. Queries $q$ arrive one at a time, revealing bids $b_{uq} \geq 0$. Each query is given to at most one advertiser, who pays his bid, or what remains of his budget if that is less. The goal is to maximize the total revenue. Under the **small-bids** assumption, every bid is small compared with every budget.
:::

Greedy, which gives each query to the highest remaining bid, is 1/2-competitive. Mehta, Saberi, Vazirani and Vazirani (2007) trade off bid and spent fraction $f_u$: give $q$ to the advertiser that maximizes
$$
b_{uq}\, \psi(f_u), \qquad \psi(f) = 1 - e^{f - 1} .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — AdWords with small bids (Mehta et al., 2007; Buchbinder, Jain and Naor, 2007)]{.tag} When the ratio of the largest bid to the smallest budget tends to 0, the algorithm above is $(1 - 1/e)$-competitive, and no deterministic algorithm does better.

::: proof
The primal–dual proof of Buchbinder, Jain and Naor works on the fractional LP, whose dual is
$$
\min \Big\{ \sum_u B_u\, \alpha_u + \sum_q \beta_q \ :\ \beta_q \geq b_{uq}\,(1 - \alpha_u)\ \ \forall u, q,\ \ \alpha, \beta \geq 0 \Big\}.
$$

1.  Keep $\alpha_u = (e^{f_u} - 1)/(e - 1)$, which grows from 0 to 1 as advertiser $u$ spends his budget. Give $q$ to the advertiser maximizing $b_{uq}(1 - \alpha_u)$, which is the rule of Mehta et al. up to a constant factor, and set $\beta_q$ to that maximum.
2.  *Dual feasibility.* $\beta_q$ covers every advertiser at the time of $q$, and $\alpha_u$ only grows afterwards, so every constraint holds at the end.
3.  *Dual growth.* When $u$ receives a small bid $b$, $f_u$ grows by $b/B_u$. The dual objective then grows by about
    $$
    B_u\, \alpha'(f_u)\, \frac{b}{B_u} + b\,(1 - \alpha_u) = \frac{b\, e^{f_u} + b\,(e - e^{f_u})}{e - 1} = \frac{e}{e - 1}\, b,
    $$
    while the revenue grows by $b$.
4.  Summing, the final dual is $e/(e-1)$ times the revenue, up to the small-bid error, and weak duality bounds the optimum by the dual. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same LP with unit bids and budgets $b$ is b-matching, and the rule becomes BALANCE. Aggarwal, Goel, Karande and Mehta (2011) handle weights on the offline vertices, with one bid per advertiser, by perturbing RANKING's priorities with $\psi$.

### 6.3 Online resource allocation by stochastic approximation

In practice, a campaign spreads its budget over the day, and queries look like i.i.d. draws from an unknown distribution. The dual of ch. 6.2 suggests a policy driven by prices: with a price $\alpha_u$ per unit of budget, give each query to the advertiser maximizing $b_{uq}(1 - \alpha_u)$, if positive.

The right prices minimize the dual. With $T$ i.i.d. queries and target spending rates $\rho_u = B_u / T$, the dual per query is the convex function
$$
D(\alpha) = \sum_u \rho_u\, \alpha_u + \mathbb{E}_q\Big[\max\big(0,\ \max_u b_{uq}(1 - \alpha_u)\big)\Big].
$$
The spending of the current query gives an unbiased stochastic subgradient, and the projected descent step is
$$
\alpha_u \leftarrow \big[\alpha_u + \eta\, (\text{spend}_u(q) - \rho_u)\big]^+ .
$$
Overspending raises an advertiser's price; underspending lowers it. This is stochastic approximation in the sense of Robbins and Monro (1951), run on the dual. Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) show that this dual descent, in mirror-descent form, has regret of order $\sqrt{T}$ under i.i.d. arrivals, so the ratio tends to 1. Devanur and Hayes (2009) learn the prices once on a first fraction of a randomly ordered input.

Under an adversarial order, learned prices can be badly wrong (Exercise 14), while the rule of Theorem 6.3 keeps $1 - 1/e$.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)

def allocate(bids, budgets, rule, eta=0.0):
    """Online AdWords: each query goes to one advertiser, who pays min(bid, remaining budget)."""
    T, m = bids.shape
    spent, alpha = np.zeros(m), np.zeros(m)
    rho = budgets / T                                # target spending rate per query
    for t in range(T):
        left = budgets - spent
        b = np.where(left > 0, np.minimum(bids[t], left), 0.0)
        if rule == "greedy":                         # highest bid
            score = b
        elif rule == "msvv":                         # b * psi(f), psi(f) = 1 - e^(f-1)
            score = b * (1 - np.exp(spent / budgets - 1))
        else:                                        # dual prices learned online
            score = b * (1 - alpha)
        u = int(np.argmax(score + 1e-9 * np.arange(m)))   # ties go to the last index
        pay = b[u] if score[u] > 0 else 0.0
        spent[u] += pay
        if rule == "dual":                           # stochastic subgradient step on the dual
            x = np.zeros(m); x[u] = pay
            alpha = np.maximum(0.0, alpha + eta * (x - rho) / rho)
    return spent.sum()

def offline_opt(bids, budgets):                     # LP relaxation = upper bound on OPT
    T, m = bids.shape
    c = -bids.ravel()                                # x[t, u] flattened
    A_q = np.kron(np.eye(T), np.ones(m))             # each query allocated at most once
    A_b = np.kron(np.ones(T), np.eye(m)) * bids.ravel()   # budget of each advertiser
    res = linprog(c, A_ub=np.vstack([A_q, A_b]), b_ub=np.r_[np.ones(T), budgets],
                  bounds=(0, 1), method="highs")
    return -res.fun

# (a) adversarial: advertisers 0..m-1, budget B; query group j is bid on by advertisers j..m-1
m, B = 10, 50
bids = np.vstack([np.tile((np.arange(m) >= j).astype(float), (B, 1)) for j in range(m)])
budgets = np.full(m, float(B))
opt = m * B
for rule in ["greedy", "msvv"]:
    print(f"(a) {rule:6s} revenue / OPT = {allocate(bids, budgets, rule) / opt:.3f}")

# (b) i.i.d. queries of two types: type X (bids 1 and 0.99), type Y (only advertiser 0 bids)
T = 2000
is_x = rng.random(T) < 0.5
bids = np.column_stack([np.ones(T), np.where(is_x, 0.99, 0.0)])
budgets = np.array([500.0, 1000.0])
lp = offline_opt(bids, budgets)
print(f"(b) offline LP bound = {lp:.1f}")
for rule, eta in [("greedy", 0), ("msvv", 0), ("dual", 0.01)]:
    print(f"(b) {rule:6s} revenue / LP = {allocate(bids, budgets, rule, eta) / lp:.3f}")
```

On the adversarial instance (a), with ties broken against the algorithm, greedy earns 0.500 of the optimum and the rule of Mehta et al. 0.658, close to $1 - (1 - 1/10)^{10} = 0.651$. On the i.i.d. instance (b), greedy spends advertiser 0's budget on queries that advertiser 1 values almost as much and earns 0.849 of the LP bound; the rule of Mehta et al. earns 0.998 and the learned prices 1.000.

### 6.4 Matching with delays

Emek, Kutten and Wattenhofer (2016) let the algorithm wait. Requests appear over time at points of a metric space and must eventually be matched in pairs; a pair costs the distance between its points, and every request pays the time it waits.

::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Neither haste nor patience is competitive]{.tag} On two points at distance $D$, let one request appear at each point at time 0, and again at time $\varepsilon$.

-   Matching as soon as two requests are pending pays $2D$, while waiting $\varepsilon$ and pairing requests at the same point costs only the waiting time $2\varepsilon$: the ratio $D/\varepsilon$ is unbounded.
-   A rule that waits for a partner at the same point pays a waiting cost that grows without bound when no other request arrives, while the optimum pays $D$ at once.
:::

A good algorithm waits until the waiting cost of a candidate pair is comparable with its distance, a rent-or-buy rule as in ski rental. On general metrics, Emek et al. combine it with a random tree embedding (ch. 8.4) and obtain a ratio polylogarithmic in the number of points and the aspect ratio; Azar, Chiplunkar and Kaplan (2017) improve the bounds.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Capacities and budgets let deterministic algorithms reach $1 - 1/e$ by balancing the spent fractions.
-   The AdWords rule weighs each bid by $\psi(f) = 1 - e^{f-1}$; its proof keeps a dual whose growth is $e/(e-1)$ times the revenue.
-   With i.i.d. queries, prices learned by stochastic subgradient steps on the dual approach the offline optimum, but they are not robust to adversarial orders.
-   Matching with delays mixes waiting costs and distances; rent-or-buy rules and tree embeddings handle it.
::::

## 7. Paging, caching and metrical task systems {#ch7}

The third family of the course moves from gains to costs. An algorithm holds a state, such as a cache content or server positions, and pays to serve requests or to change state. This chapter treats paging, then the general model of metrical task systems.

### 7.1 Paging

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Paging]{.tag} A cache holds $k$ pages out of a larger set. Requests for pages arrive one at a time. A request for a page in the cache is free; otherwise it is a **fault**, which costs 1 and brings the page in, evicting another page if the cache is full. The algorithm chooses which page to evict.
:::

The offline optimum is explicit: evicting the page whose next request is furthest in the future minimizes the number of faults (Belady, 1966), by an exchange argument.

The usual online rules are **LRU** (evict the least recently used page) and **FIFO** (evict the page that entered first). To compare them with the optimum, cut the request sequence into **phases**: each phase is a maximal segment containing requests to exactly $k$ distinct pages.

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — LRU is $k$-competitive (Sleator and Tarjan, 1985)]{.tag} For every request sequence,
$$
\mathrm{LRU} \leq k \cdot \mathrm{OPT} + k ,
$$
and no deterministic algorithm has a ratio below $k$.

::: proof
1.  *LRU pays at most $k$ per phase.* Once a page is requested in a phase, it stays among the $k$ most recently used distinct pages until the phase ends, so LRU does not evict it. Each of the $k$ pages of the phase faults at most once.
2.  *OPT pays at least 1 per phase, except the last.* Let $p$ be the first request of a phase. The rest of the phase and the first request of the next phase involve $k$ distinct pages other than $p$. Right after serving $p$, the optimum holds $p$ and only $k - 1$ other pages, so it faults at least once in that window. The windows of different phases are disjoint.
3.  *Lower bound.* With $k + 1$ pages, the adversary always requests the page missing from the algorithm's cache, so the algorithm faults at every request. Belady's rule faults at most once every $k$ requests, since the evicted page is not requested for the next $k - 1$ requests at least. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same phase argument proves that FIFO is $k$-competitive. Yet FIFO is not monotone in $k$: on the sequence 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO makes 9 faults with 3 slots and 10 with 4 slots (Belady's anomaly), while LRU makes 10 and 8.

### 7.2 Randomized paging

The **marking** algorithm works in phases too. A page is marked when it is requested; on a fault with a full cache, it evicts an unmarked page chosen uniformly at random, and when every cached page is marked, it unmarks them all and starts a new phase.

::: thm
[Theorem 7.3 — Randomized paging (Fiat et al., 1991; McGeoch and Sleator, 1991)]{.tag} The marking algorithm is $2H_k$-competitive, where $H_k = 1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/k \approx \ln k$. No randomized algorithm is better than $H_k$-competitive, and the bound $H_k$ is achieved.
:::

The proof counts, in each phase, the **new** pages, those not requested in the previous phase; say there are $m$ of them. The optimum pays at least half of the total number of new pages over all phases.

The marking algorithm pays 1 for each new page. The $j$-th old page requested in the phase has been evicted with probability at most $m/(k - j + 1)$, and summing over $j$ bounds the expected cost of the phase by $m H_k$. Randomization thus brings the ratio from $k$ down to a logarithm.

```python
import numpy as np
from collections import OrderedDict

def lru(seq, k):
    cache, faults = OrderedDict(), 0
    for p in seq:
        if p in cache:
            cache.move_to_end(p)
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(cache) == k:
            cache.popitem(last=False)        # least recently used
        cache[p] = True
    return faults

def fifo(seq, k):
    cache, order, faults = set(), [], 0
    for p in seq:
        if p not in cache:
            faults += 1
            if len(cache) == k:
                cache.remove(order.pop(0))   # first in, first out
            cache.add(p); order.append(p)
    return faults

def marking(seq, k, rng):
    cache, marked, faults = set(), set(), 0
    for p in seq:
        if p not in cache:
            faults += 1
            if len(cache) == k:
                if marked >= cache:          # every page marked: a new phase starts
                    marked = set()
                cache.remove(rng.choice(sorted(cache - marked)))
            cache.add(p)
        marked.add(p)
    return faults

def belady(seq, k):                          # offline optimum: evict the furthest next use
    cache, faults = set(), 0
    for t, p in enumerate(seq):
        if p in cache:
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(cache) == k:
            def next_use(q):
                rest = seq[t + 1:]
                return rest.index(q) if q in rest else len(seq)
            cache.remove(max(cache, key=next_use))
        cache.add(p)
    return faults

seq = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
print("k=3:", {"LRU": lru(seq, 3), "FIFO": fifo(seq, 3), "OPT": belady(seq, 3)})
print("k=4:", {"LRU": lru(seq, 4), "FIFO": fifo(seq, 4), "OPT": belady(seq, 4)})

# A cyclic scan of k+1 pages: the worst case for LRU and FIFO
k = 10
scan = list(range(k + 1)) * 30
mark = np.mean([marking(scan, k, rng) for _ in range(20)])
print(f"scan, k={k}: LRU {lru(scan, k)}, FIFO {fifo(scan, k)}, "
      f"marking {mark:.0f}, OPT {belady(scan, k)}")
```

On the cyclic scan of 11 pages with 10 slots, LRU and FIFO fault on all 330 requests, the optimum 42 times, and marking about 102 times: ratios 7.9 and 2.4, within the bounds $k = 10$ and $2H_{10} \approx 5.9$.

### 7.3 Metrical task systems

::: def
[Definition 7.4 — Metrical task system (Borodin, Linial and Saks, 1992)]{.tag} A system has $n$ states with a metric $d$ and starts in state $s_0$. At each time $t$, a task arrives as a cost vector $c_t$ over the states. The algorithm moves to a state $s_t$ and pays
$$
d(s_{t-1}, s_t) + c_t(s_t).
$$
:::

Paging is a task system whose states are the possible cache contents. The offline optimum is computed by dynamic programming on the **work function** $w_t(s)$, the least cost of serving the first $t$ tasks and ending in state $s$:
$$
w_t(s) = c_t(s) + \min_{s'} \big( w_{t-1}(s') + d(s', s) \big), \qquad w_0(s) = d(s_0, s).
$$

::: thm
[Theorem 7.5 — Task systems (Borodin, Linial and Saks, 1992; Bubeck, Coester and Rabani, 2023)]{.tag} On every metric with $n$ states, the best deterministic competitive ratio is exactly $2n - 1$. For randomized algorithms, a ratio $O(\log^2 n)$ is achievable on every metric (Bubeck, Cohen, Lee and Lee, 2019), and some metrics force $\Omega(\log^2 n)$.
:::

Good task-system algorithms balance, in each state, the task costs paid there against the cost of moving away: the rent-or-buy principle of ski rental and of ch. 6.4, applied state by state.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Belady's rule, evicting the page needed furthest in the future, is the offline optimum for paging.
-   LRU and FIFO are $k$-competitive by the phase argument, and $k$ is optimal for deterministic algorithms.
-   Random eviction among unmarked pages brings the ratio down to $O(\log k)$, and $H_k$ is optimal.
-   Metrical task systems generalize paging; work functions give the offline optimum; the deterministic ratio is $2n - 1$.
::::

## 8. The k-server problem and tree reductions {#ch8}

In the k-server problem, $k$ servers move in a metric space to cover requests, and the question is how much more than the optimum an online algorithm must move. This chapter proves the lower bound $k$, reaches it on the line, and introduces the tree reduction behind the randomized results.

### 8.1 The problem and the conjecture

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — The k-server problem (Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator, 1990)]{.tag} In a metric space $(X, d)$, $k$ servers start at given points. Each request is a point $r_t$; the algorithm must move some server to $r_t$, and pays the total distance travelled by its servers.
:::

Paging is the k-server problem on the uniform metric, where every distance is 1 and the points are the pages. The k-server problem is also a task system whose states are the configurations of the servers.

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.2 — The lower bound $k$ (Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator, 1990)]{.tag} On every metric space with at least $k + 1$ points, no deterministic online algorithm is better than $k$-competitive.

::: proof
Restrict to $k + 1$ points; every configuration then misses exactly one point.

1.  *Adversary.* Each request $r_{t+1}$ is the point the algorithm misses. The algorithm serves it from some point, which becomes the next request $r_{t+2}$; its cost is at least $\sum_t d(r_{t+1}, r_{t+2})$.
2.  *Offline algorithms.* Start $k$ offline algorithms in the $k$ configurations that contain $r_1$. On request $r_{t+1}$, the one missing it moves its server from $r_t$; the others stay.
3.  *Invariant.* The $k$ configurations remain distinct and all contain the last request: the mover now misses $r_t$, which the others contained.
4.  *Averaging.* Exactly one of them pays $d(r_t, r_{t+1})$ at each step, so together they pay the algorithm's cost up to one term. The cheapest pays at most a $1/k$ fraction, and the optimum is cheaper still. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The **k-server conjecture** states that a ratio of $k$ is achievable on every metric. It holds for $k = 2$, for $k + 1$ points, on trees and on the line, and is open in general.

### 8.2 Double Coverage on the line

**Double Coverage** (DC) serves a request outside the interval spanned by the servers with the nearest server. A request between two adjacent servers moves both towards it at the same speed, until one of them reaches it.

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.3 — DC is $k$-competitive on the line (Chrobak, Karloff, Payne and Vishwanathan, 1991)]{.tag} For every request sequence,
$$
\mathrm{DC} \leq k \cdot \mathrm{OPT} + \Phi_0 ,
$$
where $\Phi_0$ depends only on the initial positions.

::: proof
Let $M$ be the cost of a minimum matching between the servers of DC and those of OPT; on the line, matching them in sorted order is optimal. Let $S$ be the sum of the distances between pairs of DC servers. Use the potential
$$
\Phi = k\, M + S \geq 0 .
$$
At each request, OPT moves first, then DC.

1.  *OPT moves a server by $x$.* $M$ grows by at most $x$ and $S$ is unchanged, so $\Phi$ grows by at most $k x$.
2.  *DC moves one extreme server by $\delta$.* Say the request lies left of all DC servers. OPT has a server there, so the leftmost OPT server, sorted partner of the moving server, lies at the request or further left, and $M$ drops by $\delta$. The moving server gets further from the others, so $S$ grows by $(k - 1)\delta$. In total, the potential drops by the cost paid.
3.  *DC moves two neighbours by $\delta$ each.* In the sorted matching, at least one of them moves towards its partner, otherwise the OPT server at the request would be matched across them. So $M$ does not grow. The two servers get closer by $2\delta$, and for every other server one gets closer and one moves away, so $S$ drops by $2\delta$, the cost paid.
4.  Summing, the cost of DC is at most $k$ times the cost of OPT plus $\Phi_0 - \Phi_{\text{end}} \leq \Phi_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Moving the nearest server is not competitive: two close alternating requests make greedy shuttle one server forever, while the optimum brings the second server once.

```python
import numpy as np

def greedy(servers, reqs):                   # move the nearest server
    s, cost = np.array(servers, float), 0.0
    for r in reqs:
        i = np.argmin(abs(s - r))
        cost += abs(s[i] - r); s[i] = r
    return cost

def double_coverage(servers, reqs):          # DC on the line
    s, cost = np.sort(np.array(servers, float)), 0.0
    for r in reqs:
        if r <= s[0] or r >= s[-1]:          # outside the hull: nearest extreme server
            i = 0 if r <= s[0] else len(s) - 1
            cost += abs(s[i] - r); s[i] = r
        else:                                # between neighbours: both move by delta
            j = np.searchsorted(s, r)        # s[j-1] < r <= s[j]
            delta = min(r - s[j - 1], s[j] - r)
            cost += 2 * delta
            s[j - 1] += delta; s[j] -= delta
        s.sort()
    return cost

def opt_two_servers(servers, reqs):          # offline optimum for k = 2 by dynamic programming
    pts = list(servers) + list(reqs)         # after request t one server sits at reqs[t]
    a, b = servers
    V = {1: abs(a - reqs[0]), 0: abs(b - reqs[0])}   # key = index in pts of the other server
    for t in range(1, len(reqs)):
        prev, cur, W = reqs[t - 1], reqs[t], {}
        for j, c in V.items():
            W[j] = min(W.get(j, np.inf), c + abs(prev - cur))                  # move the server at prev
            W[2 + t - 1] = min(W.get(2 + t - 1, np.inf), c + abs(pts[j] - cur))  # move the other one
        V = W
    return min(V.values())

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
start = (0.0, 10.0)
trap = [4.9, 5.1] * 500 + [9.0]              # greedy oscillates, DC brings the far server in
rand = list(rng.uniform(0, 10, 300))
for name, reqs in [("trap", trap), ("random", rand)]:
    o = opt_two_servers(start, reqs)
    print(f"{name:6s}: OPT {o:7.2f}   greedy/OPT {greedy(start, reqs) / o:5.2f}"
          f"   DC/OPT {double_coverage(start, reqs) / o:4.2f}  (k = 2)")
```

On the trap, greedy pays 15 times the optimum, a ratio that grows with the length of the sequence, while DC is optimal. On 300 uniform requests greedy does better than DC (1.08 against 1.50): a competitive ratio guarantees the worst case, it does not predict typical inputs.

### 8.3 The work function algorithm

The **work function algorithm** (WFA) moves to the configuration $C$ that minimizes $w_t(C) + d(C_{t-1}, C)$, with $w_t$ the work function of ch. 7.3 on configurations: a balance between the cheapest move and the offline optimum.

::: thm
[Theorem 8.4 — WFA (Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou, 1995)]{.tag} On every metric space, the work function algorithm is $(2k - 1)$-competitive.
:::

The proof is long and is surveyed by Koutsoupias (2009). Closing the gap between $k$ and $2k - 1$ is the deterministic k-server conjecture.

### 8.4 Tree reductions

Many online problems have good algorithms on trees, and random trees transfer them to every metric.

::: def
[Definition 8.5 — Hierarchically separated tree (Bartal, 1996)]{.tag} A $\gamma$-HST is a rooted tree whose leaves are the points, with edge lengths that decrease by a factor at least $\gamma$ from each level to the next. The distance between two leaves is the length of the tree path between them.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 8.6 — Random tree embeddings (Bartal, 1996; Fakcharoenphol, Rao and Talwar, 2004)]{.tag} Every metric on $n$ points admits a probability distribution over HST metrics $d_T$ such that, for all points $x, y$,
$$
d_T(x, y) \geq d(x, y), \qquad \mathbb{E}_T\big[d_T(x, y)\big] \leq O(\log n)\, d(x, y).
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.7 — The tree reduction]{.tag} If a randomized algorithm is $\alpha$-competitive on HSTs, running it on a random tree of Theorem 8.6 is $O(\alpha \log n)$-competitive on the original metric, for any problem whose cost is a sum of distances. Indeed, distances only grow in the tree, the tree optimum is at most the tree cost of the original optimal solution, and that cost is $O(\log n)\,\mathrm{OPT}$ in expectation.
:::

Bansal, Buchbinder, Mądry and Naor (2015) gave the first randomized k-server algorithm with a ratio polylogarithmic in $k$ and $n$. Bubeck, Cohen, Lee, Lee and Mądry (2018) reached $O(\log^2 k)$ on HSTs with online mirror descent, the bridge with online learning of ch. 1.4. Bubeck, Coester and Rabani (2023) showed that some metrics force $\Omega(\log^2 k)$, refuting the conjectured $O(\log k)$.

:::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 8

-   k-server: move $k$ servers to cover requests in a metric; paging is the uniform case.
-   The averaging argument over $k$ offline algorithms proves that no deterministic ratio is below $k$.
-   Double Coverage is $k$-competitive on the line, by the potential $k M + S$.
-   The work function algorithm is $(2k-1)$-competitive everywhere; the gap to $k$ is open.
-   Random HST embeddings reduce metric problems to trees at a cost $O(\log n)$; randomized k-server needs $\Omega(\log^2 k)$ on some metrics.
::::

## 9. Convex body chasing and online transportation {#ch9}

The last in-class chapter takes metrical problems to continuous spaces and to transport.

### 9.1 Convex body chasing

::: def
